platforms.title: Your Recent Weight Change Might Be Behind Your Irregular Periods
platforms.meta_description: Blaming stress for irregular periods? A recent weight change or a jump in exercise can throw off ovulation. What actually drives it, and when to see a doctor.
platforms.body_html:
When a cycle runs 24 days one month and 38 the next, most people reach for stress as the explanation. But according to the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), a normal cycle runs 21 to 35 days, and 14% to 25% of women have irregular cycles — a large share of which trace back to a change in body weight or exercise load rather than stress alone.

Why a Change in Weight or Training Load Throws Off Ovulation

Ovulation depends on a hormone signal that runs from the hypothalamus through the pituitary gland to the ovaries. The Cleveland Clinic lists gaining or losing a significant amount of weight and "exercise routines that result in very low body fat (long-distance runners, dancers or gymnasts)" among the lifestyle factors that disrupt this signal. When calorie intake drops well below what training or daily activity demands, the hypothalamus reads it as an energy shortage and scales back the reproductive signal first.

It's not simply a low number on the scale that does this, either. In a 2016-collected sample of 808 Korean women recruited from universities and eating-disorder clinics, women who were underweight by BMI alone menstruated about as often over three months (2.66 times) as normal-weight women (2.77 times, not a significant difference), while women with anorexia nervosa menstruated only 1.21 times over the same period — a sharp, statistically significant drop. What matters is whether intake is chronically failing to match output, not the number on the scale by itself.

Skip the Scale Number — Watch the Rate of Change Instead

If you're cutting calories, the Cleveland Clinic's general guidance is to change your weight gradually rather than through diets that drastically restrict calories and food intake. If you run long distances, dance, or do gymnastics at a level that keeps body fat very low, eating enough to match that output matters more than any specific target weight. The same logic runs in reverse — a fast, large weight gain can just as easily disrupt the same hormone signal.

Logging the start date of each period on a calendar or app turns "it feels off" into an actual number of days, and makes it easier to line up a cycle change with a specific diet or training change.

This matters beyond the annoyance of not knowing when a period will show up. NICHD also notes that irregular cycles can make it harder to plan a pregnancy or rely on calendar-based birth control, since both depend on a fairly predictable ovulation date — one more reason a pattern that's actually driven by weight or training load is worth catching early rather than chalking up to stress every month.

Checklist: stress is a real factor, but so are two things people rarely check first — a recent, fast weight change and a jump in exercise volume without matching intake. Track your cycle length, and if periods stop for three months or longer and you're not pregnant, or you haven't had a period by age 16, NICHD's guidance is to see a doctor rather than wait it out — conditions like PCOS or thyroid disease need a different kind of care and a different evaluation than a lifestyle adjustment alone can provide.
